title: Getting metals from their ores
examples: How are metals extracted from ores?
How does a blast furnace work?
Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis?

explain.say: Most metals hide inside rocks called ores, joined to oxygen or sulfur. An ore is a rock with enough metal to be worth digging up. Look at the board. How you get each metal out depends on its place in the reactivity series.

Start with the easy ones. See gold and platinum? They are so unreactive that they are found pure in the ground, as nuggets or grains. You just dig and wash them out. Why do you think gold does not join with oxygen?

It is too unreactive! Now look at the middle group. Metals below carbon in the reactivity series, like iron and zinc, are freed by heating their oxides with carbon. Carbon steals the oxygen, which is called reduction. Can you tell which element does the stealing?

Carbon! Look at the blast furnace on the board. Iron ore and coke, which is nearly pure carbon, go in. Hot air makes it burn, forming carbon monoxide, which takes the oxygen from the iron oxide. Out flows molten iron. Where do you think the oxygen ends up?

stages.label: Carbon monoxide
stages.note: It takes oxygen from iron oxide.

explain.say: In carbon dioxide! Great job. Metals above carbon, like aluminium, hold oxygen too tightly, so you need electricity instead: electrolysis. Wow: aluminium was once more costly than gold, until a new electrolysis method in 1886 made it cheap.

faq.a: An ore is a rock that contains enough of a metal or metal compound to be worth extracting. Haematite is an iron ore and bauxite is an aluminium ore.
In extraction, reduction means removing oxygen from a compound. In the blast furnace, carbon monoxide reduces iron oxide to iron.
asks: What does reduced mean in chemistry?

faq.q: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis?
faq.a: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from aluminium oxide. Electricity is needed to split it.

faq.q: Why are some metals found pure?
faq.a: Very unreactive metals, like gold and platinum, do not easily join with other elements, so they stay as the pure metal in rocks and rivers.
It uses huge amounts of electricity, and the ore must be melted or dissolved at high temperatures. So aluminium is often made where power is cheap, such as hydroelectric plants in Norway and Iceland.
asks: Why does making aluminium take so much energy?

facts: Metals less reactive than carbon, such as iron and zinc, can be extracted from their oxides by heating with carbon.
The Hall–Héroult electrolysis process, invented in 1886, made aluminium cheap to produce.
